new_statements.rule_in_words: Darlong is described as a two-tone (H/L register) language; no word-stress rule is given as such. The only prominence statement is iambic: in disyllables (notably prefix/proclitic + root, e.g. /a-vɔk/ -> [ɐ.vɔk] 'his pig', /ki-pa:/ -> [kɪ.pa:] 'my father', /in-kʰai/ -> [ɪn.kʰai] 'to move') the initial open syllable is shortened and centralised, carries reduced stress and is less prominent than the following (root/final) syllable, i.e. a weak+strong sesquisyllabic pattern with prominence on the second/full syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: The reduction is stated for 'some Darlong disyllabic words'; the examples are possessive/agreement proclitics a-, ki- and the verbal prefix in-/i- before roots. Nothing is said about prominence in trisyllables (said to be the commonest word shape) or in compounds beyond tone sandhi (H+H -> H L).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (prefix/proclitic + root phonological words, citation forms elicited in fieldwork, Praat pitch tracks for tone pairs). The thesis frames suprasegmental phonology as tone + vowel length only; the stress remark sits in the syllable-typology section, so this is a tonal description with an incidental iambic-prominence observation, not a worked-out stress analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Brahma 2018 describes Darlong as spoken in Tripura (Kumarghat/Kailashahar area, Unakoti and North Tripura districts), classed by the author within Central Kuki-Chin close to Mizo/Hmar; this is the darl1242 / ISO dln variety itself, not a differently named dialect.

sources.note: Ch. 3 'Phonology' (pp. 45-99) treats suprasegmentals as tone (two register tones H/L with tone sandhi, sec. 3.2.1-3.2.3) and vowel length (3.2.4); there is no stress section and the word 'stress' occurs once: sec. 3.1.5.4-3.1.5.5 (p. 92) says the initial open syllable of some disyllables is shortened/centralised and 'reduces stress and relatively less prominent than the following syllable', and that Darlong words pattern as sesquisyllabic 'weak syllable followed by a strong syllable' (iambic). Ch. 2 states 'There are no available linguistic researches on Darlong language.'
